newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler adds dealer incentive to spur March car sales.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler adds dealer incentive to spur March car sales.

text.p: Two days after Chrysler Corp. reported a nearly 7 percent drop in February car sales, industry analysts said Wednesday the automaker is offering dealer incentives that will cost it $575 a car.

The news prompted analysts to trim their first-quarter and full-year earnings estimates for Chrysler amid warnings that competitive pressure from Japanese automakers could squeeze profit margins at Detroit's Big Three as the year wears on.
Chrysler's stock price fell 75 cents to $31.25 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
The new programme, which is not being offered directly to the public, only covers cars and is scheduled to end toward the end of March, they said.
Goldman Sachs analyst James Irwin and Salomon Brothers analyst Jack Kirnan both trimmed their earnings estimates.

"It should be noted that dealer programmes tend to be less effective than pure retail initiatives, and the new programme is the second major programme undertaken by Chrysler within the past 30 days," Kirnan said in a research report.
A Chrysler spokesman refused to comment, citing a company policy against discussing dealer incentives.
Chrysler's total sales were down 2.8 percent in February on a daily sales basis.

General Motors Corp. and Ford Motor Co. also suffered slumps in car sales that dragged down their overall monthly sales results from a year ago. The Big Three sales slide came at the same time that Toyota Motor Corp., Honda Motor Co. Ltd. and Nissan Motor Co. Ltd. reported strong sales and gains in market share.

The February results point to troubling signs for domestic automakers at a time when the Japanese are using the weak yen to set aggressive prices and improve their market share, analysts said. This year may prove to be healthy for sales, but could be difficult for profit margins as the Big Three are forced to keep pace with price discounts, they said.
GM, which has taken a cautious approach to ramping up new car production, suffered declines in its normally robust pickup truck and sport utility business despite ample inventories.
Chevrolet C/K pickup sales were down 2.8 percent to 41,688, while sales of the Tahoe full-size sport utility plunged 16.3 percent to 9,468.

GM officials have repeatedly said sales comparisons will improve in the second half of the year when production of its new car and minivan models is in full swing. But some analysts believe that excuse is wearing thin.

"I would not hang my hat on the fact that by the time GM gets all these vehicles out there, they're going to be able to reclaim their market share," said George Magliano, an analyst at WEFA Group, an industry consulting firm.
"The Japanese are tough competitors right now and they are not going to give up easily," he said.

However, Goldman analyst Irwin said GM was better positioned than Ford or Chrysler. Total industry vehicle sales for 1997 are expected to remain strong throughout the year at 15.4 million units, providing GM with plenty of buyers for its new products once they arrive.
"GM, at least from a competitive standpoint and a profit standpoint, will be in a stronger position as the year unfolds. That is something Chrysler can't count on, or Ford," he said.
